Package org.aeonbits.owner.validation

Class Constraints

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.validation.Constraints
public final class Constraints extends Object
Recognises a Bean Validation constraint by name, which is how the core can know that a configuration carries constraints while depending on no validation API at all.

An annotation is a constraint when it is itself annotated with javax.validation.Constraint or jakarta.validation.Constraint - which is what the specification requires of every constraint, the built-in ones, the composed ones and the ones written by hand alike. Nothing here loads either class: the meta-annotations are already there to be read, and only their names are compared. A class path without a validation API has no constraint annotations on it either, since they would not resolve, and this answers false for everything.

Why the core cares at all. It cannot check a constraint, and it does not try. It has to be able to see one, because a @Min(12) that nothing validates is the failure this whole mechanism exists to prevent: it reads like a guarantee and is not one. Seeing it is what lets the library say so.

2.0.0

  • Method Details

    • anyOn

      public static boolean anyOn(Method method)
      Tells whether the given method carries any constraint at all - on the method itself, as in @Min(12) int port(), or on a type argument of its return type, as in Optional<@Min(12) Integer> port().

      Both shapes have to be looked at, and the second one is the easy one to forget: a constraint written inside the angle brackets is not among AccessibleObject.getAnnotations() at all, so a method whose only constraint is a container element constraint would look unannotated and would be passed over in silence - which is the one outcome not allowed here.

      Parameters:
      method - the method to inspect.
      Returns:
      true if the method carries at least one Bean Validation constraint.

    • anyDeclaredOn

      public static boolean anyDeclaredOn(Method method)
      Tells whether the given method carries a constraint written on the method itself, as opposed to one written on a type argument of its return type.

      The distinction is not academic for a method returning an Optional or a collection: a constraint written on the method applies to the container, and a container is never null and never absent. See ConfigValidator for what is reported about it.

      Parameters:
      method - the method to inspect.
      Returns:
      true if a constraint annotation is present on the method itself.

    • isConstraint

      public static boolean isConstraint(Class<? extends Annotation> type)
      Tells whether the given annotation type is a Bean Validation constraint.
      Parameters:
      type - the annotation type to inspect, never null.
      Returns:
      true if it is annotated with either spelling of @Constraint.
